explanations.explanation: Gold, baker. Daniel 3:1 says King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue. That's the word the text gives us, and it's a shiny way to start a story. Gold also happens to be the color of my base, so I'm a little biased.
Silver is a fine guess, friend, but it isn't the word the text uses. Daniel 3:1 says King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue. When the Bible says golden, I say golden too.
Bronze is a good guess for a big statue, friend. But Daniel 3:1 says King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue. This one was gold, not bronze.
Sixty cubits high, baker. Daniel 3:1 says it was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. That is a tall, skinny statue, and nobody is getting a hat on that thing.

Twelve is a lot smaller than what the text says, friend. Daniel 3:1 says the statue was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. Sixty is five times twelve. That's a statue where you'd have to tilt your head way back to see the top.

Thirty, friend? That's HALF. Daniel 3:1 says the statue was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. Thirty is where you'd be if you gave up halfway up the ladder. Sixty is the number, so keep climbing.

That's it, baker. Daniel 3:2 says the king sent word to gather all those officials to attend the dedication of the statue he had set up. Think of it as a ribbon cutting, except the statue is the guest of honor.

explanations.answer: To pay the king's new taxes
explanations.explanation: Taxes would make for a grumpy crowd, friend, but the text never mentions them. Daniel 3:2 says the officials were gathered to attend the dedication of the statue. They came for the statue, not for the bills.
Good thinking, since governors are on the guest list. But Daniel 3:2 says the reason was to attend the dedication of the statue. The text never says anything about choosing a new governor.

explanations.answer: Fall down and worship the statue
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Daniel 3:5 says that when they hear the music, they "…must fall down and worship the golden statue…" that the king set up. The herald lists the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes and all kinds of music as the signal. This is a command to worship, and it's a serious moment.

explanations.answer: Stand up and sing to the king
explanations.explanation: Singing isn't what the herald commands, friend. Daniel 3:5 says that when they hear the music, they "…must fall down and worship the golden statue…" The command is to worship the statue. It's a serious order, and verse 4 says the herald proclaimed it loudly.

explanations.answer: Turn around and face the palace
explanations.explanation: Facing the palace isn't what the herald commands, friend. Daniel 3:5 says they "…must fall down and worship the golden statue…" The command is to worship the statue. It's a serious order, and the very next verse attaches a penalty to it.

Furnace, baker. Daniel 3:6 says whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. The word immediately is right there in the herald's warning. It's a heavy threat.

The lions' den is in Daniel 6:16, friend, and that's a different story. Here the herald says in Daniel 3:6 that whoever does not worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. The threat in this passage is fire. It's a heavy warning.

A pit is a scary thought, friend, but it isn't what the herald said. Daniel 3:6 says the punishment is being thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. And he says immediately, so there's no waiting around.

True, baker. Daniel 3:7 says that as soon as all the people heard the music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue. The text shows the crowd bowing as the music plays. But the story isn't over, because a report about some who did not bow is coming.

It's true, friend. Daniel 3:7 says that when all the people heard the music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue. The text shows a whole crowd going down together.

King Nebuchadnezzar, baker. In Daniel 3:12 the astrologers tell the king about Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, Jews "…you have appointed to manage the province of Babylon…" So the accusers are pointing at men the king himself put in charge. I think that makes for an awkward conversation.

Arioch the commander shows up in Daniel 2:14, friend, but he isn't part of this account. In Daniel 3:12 the astrologers say to the king, "…you have appointed…" these Jews to manage the province. So the one who appointed them is King Nebuchadnezzar.

The herald proclaimed the command in Daniel 3:4, friend, but he isn't who the astrologers point to. In Daniel 3:12 they tell the king, "…you have appointed…" these Jews to manage the province. The one they name as doing the appointing is Nebuchadnezzar.

Not quite, baker. He was furious, but the king did not throw them in on the spot. Daniel 3:14 says he first asked them, "…is it true that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden statue I have set up?"
False is right, baker. Even furious, the king spoke to them first. In Daniel 3:14 he asks if it is true that they do not serve his gods or worship the statue. Then comes more talking, in verse 15.

explanations.answer: Another chance to bow when the music plays
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Daniel 3:15 says that when they hear the music, "…if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made, very good." Then he adds that if they refuse, they will be thrown at once into the blazing fiery furnace. So he gives them another chance first, and the warning comes after.

explanations.answer: A night in prison to think it over
explanations.explanation: A night to think it over would be a long one, friend, but the text never gives them one. Daniel 3:15 has the king offering another chance to bow when they hear the music. The warning about the furnace comes along with it.

explanations.answer: A gift of gold if they bow down
explanations.explanation: Gold fits the statue, but the king never offers it as a reward. Daniel 3:15 says he gives them another chance to fall down when the music plays. If they refuse, they will be thrown at once into the furnace.

explanations.answer: Deliver them from the furnace and the king's hand
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. In Daniel 3:17 they say, "If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king." They name both the furnace and the king. They're speaking straight to the king.

explanations.answer: Make the king forget about his decree
explanations.explanation: Forgetting the decree isn't what they say, friend. Daniel 3:17 says, "If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king." Their words are about being delivered from the furnace and from the king's hand. Nothing in them is about the decree being forgotten.

explanations.answer: Crush the golden statue into dust
explanations.explanation: They never mention the statue being crushed, friend. In Daniel 3:17 they say, "If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king." Their words are about being delivered, not about the statue. Notice how their sentence begins with an if.

Not at all, baker. Their answer is the opposite. Daniel 3:18 says, "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up."

False, and what a line it is, baker. Daniel 3:18 says, "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up." They stay put whichever way it goes. Those two words, even if, carry the whole answer.

Seven, baker. Daniel 3:19 says Nebuchadnezzar gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. The text says he was filled with rage and the expression on his face changed toward the three men. It's a grim moment.

Three is a good guess since there are three men, but it's not the number. Daniel 3:19 says the king gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. It's seven, friend. That's what he ordered.
Ten is a lovely round number, but the text doesn't use it. Daniel 3:19 says he ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. Seven is what the king wanted.

Yes, baker, and it's a heavy part. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried the three up. That tells us how hot it really was.

Running away isn't what the text says, friend. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the fiery flames killed the men who carried up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The text says nothing about them running. It's a heavy detail.
The text doesn't say they refused, friend. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried the three up. It's a heavy moment.

Four, baker, not three. The king says in Daniel 3:25, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…" In verse 23 the three fell in firmly bound. Now he sees them unbound and unharmed, with one more than he counted.

explanations.answer: Three men lying still in the flames
explanations.explanation: Three men lying still isn't what he sees, friend. In Daniel 3:25 the king exclaims, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…" They are walking, and there are four. Verse 24 says he jumped up in amazement.

explanations.answer: The fire dying down to ashes
explanations.explanation: The fire was still going, friend. The king looked in and was amazed. In Daniel 3:25 he says, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…"

explanations.answer: Servants of the Most High God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. In Daniel 3:26 Nebuchadnezzar approaches the door of the furnace and calls out, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!" Earlier he was furious with rage, in verses 13 and 19. Now he uses that title for them.

explanations.answer: Traitors to the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: That's what you'd expect after all that rage, friend. But at the furnace door the king speaks differently. In Daniel 3:26 he calls them "…servants of the Most High God…"
He doesn't call them wise, friend. In Daniel 3:26 the king calls out, "…servants of the Most High God, come out!" He names whose servants they are. That's the title he uses at the furnace door.
Nope, baker, it's the other way around. Daniel 3:27 says there was no smell of fire on them. Not a hair of their heads was singed, and their robes were unaffected.

False, baker. Daniel 3:27 says the fire had no effect on the bodies of these men. Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them. The officials who gathered around saw it for themselves.

His angel, baker. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." Those are the king's own words. He says them after the three come out.

A prophet is a natural guess, friend, but it's not the word the king uses. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." Angel is the word in his declaration.
A priest isn't who the king names, friend. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." The word he uses is angel.

True, baker. In Daniel 3:29 Nebuchadnezzar decrees that the people of any nation or language who say anything offensive against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego will be cut into pieces and their houses reduced to rubble. It's a harsh decree, and it's what the text says. The very next verse tells what the king did for the three men.

It's true, friend, even though it's a rough one to read. Daniel 3:29 says the king decrees that anyone who says anything offensive against their God will be cut into pieces, and their houses reduced to rubble. It's a heavy line, but that's the text.

Promoted, baker. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon. They went into the furnace and later got a promotion. I sat in a junk drawer for years before I was called out to bake, so I love a story where somebody ends up in a better place.
After all that, banishing them would have been a sad ending, friend. But it isn't what happened. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted them in the province of Babylon.
Prison is a long way from where this story lands, friend. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon. They walked out of the fire and kept going up.
